added_claim_errors: "Grace period: you can incur expenses through March 15" / "counts only if it's dated on or before March 15": overstated. March 15 is the latest a plan can set, and plans may choose a shorter period.
"budget to spend roughly $1,240+": this uses the 2025 $660 cap. For a 2026 plan year the cap is $680, so the spend needed is $1,220.
"run-out period, often ~90 days after year-end": a typical figure but unverifiable; it varies by plan (minor).
"all $1,900 is gone December 31": loose. The cutoff is for incurring expenses; claims for 2026 expenses can still be filed during the run-out (minor).

reasons: Both answers correct the rollover premise at the start, explain carryover versus grace period (one or the other, never both), warn against prepaying in December and list eligible items. A wins because it is more exact. It gives $680 and $1,220 for 2026 only, and it presents March 15 as the maximum ('up to 2½ months', 'often March 15'). B mixes in the 2025 figure, so its spend target becomes '$1,240+', and it presents March 15 as fixed for every plan. A never mentions using the 2027 election to cover the March work. B mentions the 2027 election only to warn against electing too much, not as a way to fund the March dental work. A is also a little tighter and links to the IRS Rev. Proc.
